notes.front: What is the CNCF TOC?
notes.back: The CNCF’s Technical Oversight Committee, which evaluates projects against each maturity level’s criteria and votes on moving them up.
notes.explanation: Its evaluation is called due diligence; it decides whether a project is ready for the next level.
notes.example: A project applying to graduate is assigned a TOC sponsor, who reviews it and interviews its adopters.
notes.source: CNCF TOC, “CNCF Project Lifecycle & Process”, “Project Lifecycle Process”
notes.sourceLicence: C · no licence found; facts in our own words

notes.front: What are the CNCF project maturity levels?
notes.back: The lifecycle stages the TOC defines for CNCF projects, from experimental Sandbox, through Incubation, to production-proven Graduated.
notes.explanation: A project’s level tells adopters how stable and widely proven it is. Archived is a fourth stage for inactive projects.
notes.example: Kubernetes is a Graduated project; a brand-new CNCF project usually starts in Sandbox.
notes.sourceLicence: C · no licence found; facts in our own words
notes.validAsOf: 2026-09-25 · CNCF documents as of that date

image.alt: CNCF project stages. Sandbox: experimental, early in development, breaking changes likely. Then Incubation: gaining adoption, more stable versioned APIs. Then Graduated: highly mature and production-proven by its adopters. Projects join at Sandbox or apply directly for Incubation; the TOC checks each move by due diligence, then votes. Archived, shown apart, is for inactive or no longer recommended projects.
image.credit: Drawn for this deck from CNCF TOC, “CNCF Project Lifecycle & Process” (facts from a tier-C source, in our own words)

notes.front: What is the CNCF Landscape?
notes.back: A map that tries to categorise most cloud native projects and product offerings, placing each in the one category where it fits best.
notes.explanation: The README calls it “a map through the previously uncharted terrain of cloud native technologies”; CNCF projects are one well-travelled path through it.
notes.example: Looking for a service mesh? The Landscape groups the options in one category, with CNCF projects marked.
notes.validAsOf: 2026-09-25 · CNCF documents as of that date

notes.front: What is a SIG in the Kubernetes project?
notes.back: A Special Interest Group: community members who together manage an ongoing area of the project, such as networking or documentation.
notes.explanation: The project is organised mainly into SIGs, and every identifiable part of it, from repositories to APIs and tests, is meant to be owned by one.
notes.example: SIG Network owns Pod networking, Services (including kube-proxy), Ingress, DNS and network policy.

notes.front: What is a working group (WG) in the Kubernetes project?
notes.back: A group for a short-lived, narrow or cross-SIG topic, organising people to accomplish a discrete task.
notes.explanation: WGs are rallying points for topics that cross SIG lines, without creating a new permanent SIG.
notes.example: Several SIGs need a shared approach to one narrow problem for a few months, so they form a WG.

notes.front: What is a committee in Kubernetes governance?
notes.back: A group for topics that need discretion, such as security or code of conduct; its membership is closed and decided by the Steering Committee.
notes.explanation: Unlike SIGs, committees are not open for anyone to join and do not always work in the open. The Steering Committee is where unresolved decisions are finally escalated.
notes.example: A code-of-conduct complaint needs discretion, so a committee handles it rather than an open SIG.

notes.front: What is a KEP?
notes.back: A Kubernetes Enhancement Proposal: the process for defining, agreeing and communicating significant changes, especially ones that cross SIG boundaries.
notes.explanation: Enhancements are tracked in the kubernetes/enhancements repository, owned by SIG Architecture, and usually take several releases to complete.
notes.example: A feature moving from beta to GA, or a new API needing work from several SIGs, is tracked as an enhancement.
notes.source: Kubernetes community, “Kubernetes Community Governance Model”, “Cross-project Communication and Coordination”; Kubernetes Enhancements repository, README

notes.front: In the Kubernetes glossary, who is a contributor?
notes.back: Someone who donates code, documentation or their time to help the Kubernetes project or community.
notes.explanation: Contributions include pull requests, issues, feedback, SIG participation and organising community events.
notes.example: Someone who fixes a mistake in the Kubernetes docs through a pull request is a contributor.

notes.front: In the Kubernetes glossary, who is a member?
notes.back: A continuously active contributor, who can be assigned issues and pull requests and takes part in SIGs through GitHub teams.
notes.explanation: Pre-submit tests run automatically on members’ pull requests; members are expected to stay active.
notes.example: A contributor who has been active for months joins the GitHub team for their SIG and becomes a member.

notes.front: In the Kubernetes glossary, who is a reviewer?
notes.back: Someone who reviews code for quality and correctness on some part of the project.
notes.explanation: Reviewers know both the codebase and software engineering principles; reviewer status is scoped to part of the codebase.
notes.example: A reviewer for the scheduler code checks a pull request’s logic and tests.

notes.front: In the Kubernetes glossary, who is an approver?
notes.back: Someone who can review and approve code contributions, judging their holistic acceptance; approvers were previously called maintainers.
notes.explanation: Holistic acceptance covers compatibility, API and flag conventions, subtle performance issues and interactions with the rest of the system.
notes.example: After review, an approver confirms a change keeps backwards compatibility and approves it for merging.

notes.front: What is a CLA?
notes.back: A Contributor License Agreement: the terms under which a contributor grants an open-source project a licence for their contributions.
notes.explanation: CLAs help resolve legal disputes over contributed material and intellectual property. All Kubernetes contributors must sign the CNCF CLA.
notes.example: A first-time contributor signs the CNCF CLA before contributing code to Kubernetes.
notes.source: Kubernetes documentation, Glossary, “CLA (Contributor License Agreement)”; Kubernetes Community Governance Model, “CLA”

notes.front: In the Kubernetes community, what does “upstream” mean?
notes.back: The core Kubernetes codebase that the wider ecosystem relies on; in git, the source repository a fork came from.
notes.explanation: Moving a feature upstream means putting it into the core codebase rather than a plugin or third-party tool.
notes.example: A feature first built in a third-party plugin is later moved upstream into core Kubernetes.

notes.front: In the Kubernetes community, what does “downstream” mean?
notes.back: The ecosystem, code and third-party tools that rely on the core Kubernetes codebase; in git, a forked repository.
notes.explanation: A new Kubernetes feature may be adopted downstream by applications that build on it.
notes.example: A vendor’s Kubernetes distribution built on the core code is downstream of it.

notes.front: What are open standards in the Kubernetes ecosystem?
notes.back: Shared specifications, such as CRI, CNI and CSI, that let different vendors’ runtimes and plugins work with Kubernetes.
notes.explanation: Because each interface is shared, a runtime, network plugin or storage driver that follows it can in principle be swapped without changing Kubernetes (our inference).
notes.example: CSI lets a storage vendor ship a driver for Kubernetes without adding it to the Kubernetes repository.
notes.source: Kubernetes documentation, Glossary, “Container Storage Interface (CSI)”, “Container Runtime Interface (CRI)” and “Container network interface (CNI)”; “open standards” is the KCNA curriculum’s term

notes.front: What kind of projects does the CNCF build ecosystems and a community around?
notes.back: Projects that orchestrate containers, such as Kubernetes.
notes.explanation: It hosts key parts of the cloud native software stack and is a neutral home for collaboration; Kubernetes is a CNCF project.
notes.example: Kubernetes, Prometheus, Fluentd and gRPC are all hosted by the CNCF.
notes.source: Kubernetes documentation, Glossary, “Cloud Native Computing Foundation (CNCF)”; KCNA Exam Curriculum, page 3

notes.front: Which organisation is the CNCF part of?
notes.back: The Linux Foundation, a nonprofit organisation.
notes.explanation: The CNCF brings together developers, end users and vendors, and serves as a neutral home for collaboration.

notes.front: The KCNA curriculum names six CNCF-hosted projects: Kubernetes, Fluentd, Linkerd, Prometheus, OpenTracing and {{c1::gRPC}}.
notes.explanation: gRPC is a way for programs to talk to each other over a network, in a compact message format.

notes.front: The CNCF’s KCNA page names three key CNCF projects beyond Kubernetes. Which?
notes.back: Prometheus, Envoy and Fluentd.
notes.explanation: Prometheus is for monitoring and alerting, Envoy is an edge and service proxy, and Fluentd routes and transforms logs.
notes.source: CNCF, “Kubernetes and Cloud Native Associate (KCNA)”, “The KCNA certification validates”; Envoy documentation, “What is Envoy”

notes.front: What is Kubernetes’ CNCF maturity level?
notes.back: Graduated.
notes.explanation: The kubernetes.io home page says: “We are a CNCF graduated project”.
notes.validAsOf: 2026-09-25 · Kubernetes docs as of that date

notes.front: What CNCF maturity level has KEDA reached?
notes.back: Graduated.
notes.explanation: KEDA scales workloads on events, such as the number of messages in a queue.
notes.validAsOf: 2026-09-25 · Kubernetes docs as of that date

notes.front: When did Prometheus join the CNCF, and in what position?
notes.back: In 2016, as the second hosted project, after Kubernetes.
notes.explanation: Joining emphasised that Prometheus is maintained independently of any company.

notes.front: Which two projects merged to form OpenTelemetry, now a CNCF project?
notes.back: OpenTracing and OpenCensus.
notes.explanation: Both tried to standardise how code is instrumented and telemetry sent to a backend; neither solved it alone.

notes.front: In the CNCF lifecycle, what is a Sandbox project?
notes.back: An experimental or innovative project early in its development; failure and significant, even breaking, changes are possible.
notes.explanation: A few organisations may still use one in production, case by case.
notes.source: CNCF TOC, “CNCF Project Lifecycle & Process”, “Project stages”
notes.sourceLicence: C · no licence found; facts in our own words
notes.validAsOf: 2026-09-25 · CNCF documents as of that date

notes.front: In the CNCF lifecycle, what is an Incubating project?
notes.back: One gaining adoption and stability, with fewer breaking changes and more stable, versioned APIs; the TOC begins actively evaluating its adoption.
notes.explanation: It is the middle stage of CNCF project maturity.
notes.source: CNCF TOC, “CNCF Project Lifecycle & Process”, “Project stages”
notes.sourceLicence: C · no licence found; facts in our own words
notes.validAsOf: 2026-09-25 · CNCF documents as of that date

notes.front: In the CNCF lifecycle, what is a Graduated project?
notes.back: A highly mature, robust project whose adopters have shown it is production-ready; the top of the maturity levels.
notes.explanation: Graduation signals stability, security practices and active community engagement.
notes.source: CNCF TOC, “CNCF Project Lifecycle & Process”, “Project stages”
notes.sourceLicence: C · no licence found; facts in our own words
notes.validAsOf: 2026-09-25 · CNCF documents as of that date

notes.front: In the CNCF lifecycle, what is an Archived project?
notes.back: An inactive project, or one that is no longer recommended for use.
notes.explanation: Archiving keeps the community focused on active, impactful projects.
notes.source: CNCF TOC, “CNCF Project Lifecycle & Process”, “Project stages”
notes.sourceLicence: C · no licence found; facts in our own words
notes.validAsOf: 2026-09-25 · CNCF documents as of that date

notes.front: How can a project enter the CNCF?
notes.back: By applying as a Sandbox project, or by applying directly for Incubation.
notes.explanation: So a project need not start in Sandbox.
notes.source: CNCF TOC, “CNCF Project Lifecycle & Process”, “Project Lifecycle Process”
notes.sourceLicence: C · no licence found; facts in our own words
notes.validAsOf: 2026-09-25 · CNCF documents as of that date

notes.front: What is the TOC’s evaluation of whether a project meets a level’s criteria called?
notes.back: Due diligence.
notes.explanation: It checks that the project’s work meets the outcome and intent the TOC set for that level.
notes.source: CNCF TOC, “CNCF Project Lifecycle & Process”, “Project Lifecycle Process”
notes.sourceLicence: C · no licence found; facts in our own words
notes.validAsOf: 2026-09-25 · CNCF documents as of that date

notes.front: What vote moves a CNCF project to Incubation or Graduation?
notes.back: A two-thirds supermajority of the TOC, after a two-week public comment period.
notes.explanation: The vote is held on the due diligence pull request, and community members may show support too.
notes.source: CNCF TOC, “CNCF Project Lifecycle & Process”, “Voting is completed”
notes.sourceLicence: C · no licence found; facts in our own words
notes.validAsOf: 2026-09-25 · CNCF documents as of that date

notes.front: What rough bar does the CNCF Landscape set for including an open-source project?
notes.back: A cloud native project with at least 300 GitHub stars that clearly fits an existing category.
notes.explanation: Each entry goes in the single category where it fits best.
notes.validAsOf: 2026-09-25 · CNCF documents as of that date

notes.front: Into which three types of subgroup is the Kubernetes project organised?
notes.back: SIGs (with their subprojects), working groups and committees.
notes.explanation: SIGs own ongoing areas, WGs handle short-lived or cross-SIG topics, and committees handle matters needing discretion.
notes.source: Kubernetes community, “Kubernetes Community Governance Model”, “Community groups”

notes.front: Within a SIG, what are subprojects?
notes.back: Specific work efforts; every part of the Kubernetes code and documentation must be owned by some subproject.
notes.explanation: Subproject owners are technical leaders for vision, design and approving KEP approvers.

notes.front: How many chairs must a Kubernetes SIG have?
notes.back: At least one, and ideally two, at any time.
notes.explanation: Chairs organise and facilitate, and coordinate with other SIGs and the Steering Committee.

notes.front: SIGs can be vertical, horizontal or project SIGs. What is an example of each?
notes.back: Vertical: Network or Storage. Horizontal: Scalability or Architecture. Project: Testing, Release or Docs.
notes.explanation: Vertical SIGs focus on components, horizontal ones cut across many areas, and project SIGs support the project itself.

notes.front: Where does an extended cross-SIG debate or deadlock go?
notes.back: To the Steering Committee, which is expected to be uncommon; normally the SIG that owns the area decides.
notes.explanation: SIGs are expected to coordinate and reach mutually agreed solutions first.
notes.source: Kubernetes community, “Kubernetes Community Governance Model”, “Cross-project Communication and Coordination”

notes.front: When may a Kubernetes enhancement be filed?
notes.back: Once there is consensus in at least one Kubernetes SIG.
notes.explanation: Circulate the idea first, in community or SIG meetings, mailing lists or an issue.

notes.front: Which kinds of change are unlikely to count as a Kubernetes enhancement? Give three.
notes.back: For example: fixing a flaky test, refactoring code, or adding error messages or events.
notes.explanation: Features implemented with a CustomResourceDefinition, and speed-ups only visible as faster API calls, are also unlikely to count.
notes.source: Kubernetes Enhancements repository, README, “Is My Thing an Enhancement?”

notes.front: In a Kubernetes release cycle, when does Code Freeze start, and how long does it last?
notes.back: Around week 12, for about two weeks; only critical bug fixes are accepted.
notes.explanation: About two more weeks follow before release, to resolve remaining critical issues and finalise documentation.
notes.source: Kubernetes documentation, “Kubernetes Release Cycle”, “The Release Cycle”
notes.validAsOf: 2026-09-25 · Kubernetes docs as of that date

notes.front: When does Enhancements Freeze start in a Kubernetes release cycle?
notes.back: About four weeks into the cycle.
notes.explanation: By then all feature work intended for the release must be defined in planning artifacts.
notes.source: Kubernetes documentation, “Kubernetes Release Cycle”, “The Release Cycle”
notes.validAsOf: 2026-09-25 · Kubernetes docs as of that date

notes.front: Which open standard defines the protocol between the kubelet and the container runtime?
notes.back: CRI, the Container Runtime Interface: a gRPC protocol.
notes.explanation: containerd and CRI-O both implement it.

notes.front: Network plugins that follow which specification provide Pod networking in Kubernetes?
notes.back: CNI, the Container Network Interface.
notes.explanation: CNI plugins are a type of network plugin that adheres to the CNI specification.

notes.front: Which open standard lets storage vendors write out-of-tree storage plugins for Kubernetes?
notes.back: CSI, the Container Storage Interface.
notes.explanation: A deployed CSI driver can then be used through a StorageClass.

notes.front: Which specification defines the format of the image digests Kubernetes uses?
notes.back: The OCI Image Specification.
notes.explanation: A digest identifies one exact image, unlike a tag, which can move.

notes.front: A new project has an innovative idea, frequent breaking changes and a handful of early adopters. At which level would it most likely join the CNCF?
notes.back: Sandbox.
notes.choices:
A) Sandbox
B) Incubation
C) Graduated
notes.choicesExplained: B: Incubation needs a slower rate of change and more stable, versioned APIs. C: Graduated needs proven production use by adopters.
notes.explanation: Sandbox is for experimental, early-stage projects where failure is still possible.
notes.source: CNCF TOC, “CNCF Project Lifecycle & Process”, “Project stages”
notes.sourceLicence: C · no licence found; facts in our own words
notes.validAsOf: 2026-09-25 · CNCF documents as of that date

notes.front: A CNCF project has left its experimental phase: breaking changes are rarer and its APIs are versioned, but it is not yet widely proven in production. Which level fits?
notes.back: Incubation.
notes.choices:
A) Sandbox
B) Incubation
C) Graduated
notes.choicesExplained: A: it is no longer experimental. C: Graduated projects have adopters who have shown production readiness.
notes.explanation: Incubation is the middle stage: stable and gaining adoption, but short of Graduated maturity.
notes.source: CNCF TOC, “CNCF Project Lifecycle & Process”, “Project stages”
notes.sourceLicence: C · no licence found; facts in our own words
notes.validAsOf: 2026-09-25 · CNCF documents as of that date

notes.front: Who decides whether an Incubating CNCF project becomes Graduated, and how?
notes.back: The TOC, after due diligence, by a two-thirds supermajority vote.
notes.explanation: A TOC sponsor reviews the project against the graduation criteria before the vote.
notes.source: CNCF TOC, “CNCF Project Lifecycle & Process”, “Voting is completed”
notes.sourceLicence: C · no licence found; facts in our own words
notes.validAsOf: 2026-09-25 · CNCF documents as of that date

notes.front: An architect wants to use only CNCF projects proven in production. Do Kubernetes and KEDA qualify?
notes.back: Yes: both are Graduated projects.
notes.explanation: Graduated is the maturity level for projects whose adopters have shown production readiness.
notes.source: Kubernetes home page, kubernetes.io; Kubernetes documentation, “Autoscaling Workloads”, “Event driven Autoscaling” (“KEDA is a CNCF-graduated project”)
notes.validAsOf: 2026-09-25 · Kubernetes docs as of that date

notes.front: You need to see which projects and products exist in one cloud native category, and where CNCF projects sit among them. Which CNCF resource do you use?
notes.back: The CNCF Landscape.
notes.explanation: It categorises most cloud native projects and product offerings.
notes.validAsOf: 2026-09-25 · CNCF documents as of that date

notes.front: You need a CNCF project to collect container logs on every node and route them to several destinations. Which of the key projects fits?
notes.back: Fluentd.
notes.choices:
A) Prometheus
B) Envoy
C) Fluentd
notes.choicesExplained: A: Prometheus is a metrics monitoring and alerting toolkit. B: Envoy is an edge and service proxy, not a logging tool; Fluentd is on the docs’ list of logging tools.
notes.explanation: The Kubernetes docs list Fluentd as a node-level logging agent that routes and transforms logs.
notes.source: Kubernetes documentation, “Observability”, “Logging tools”; Envoy documentation, “What is Envoy”

notes.front: You want to contribute a change to kube-proxy. Which Kubernetes group owns that area?
notes.back: SIG Network.
notes.choices:
A) SIG Network
B) A working group
C) The Steering Committee
notes.choicesExplained: B: WGs handle short-lived or cross-SIG topics; ownership of each part of the project sits with a SIG. C: the Steering Committee handles escalations, not day-to-day ownership.
notes.explanation: SIG Network’s subprojects include Pod networking, Services (including kube-proxy), Ingress, DNS and network policy.

notes.front: Contributors from SIG Node and SIG Scheduling need to work together for a few months on one narrow question. What kind of group fits?
notes.back: A working group (WG).
notes.choices:
A) A new SIG
B) A WG
C) A committee
notes.choicesExplained: A: a SIG owns an ongoing area, not a short-lived question. C: committees handle matters needing discretion and have closed membership.
notes.explanation: WGs exist for short-lived topics that cross SIG lines.
notes.source: Kubernetes community, “Kubernetes Community Governance Model”, “Working Groups”

notes.front: A sensitive code-of-conduct matter must be handled discreetly. Which kind of Kubernetes group deals with it?
notes.back: A committee.
notes.explanation: Committees exist for topics needing discretion; SIGs and WGs work in the open.

notes.front: You propose a feature that changes the Kubernetes API and needs work from three SIGs over several releases. What do you write?
notes.back: A KEP, tracked in the kubernetes/enhancements repository.
notes.explanation: Enhancements that need several SIGs, change the API or take several releases are exactly what KEPs are for.
notes.source: Kubernetes Enhancements repository, README, “Is My Thing an Enhancement?”

notes.front: A storage vendor wants its product usable from Kubernetes without adding code to the Kubernetes repository. Which standard does it implement?
notes.back: CSI.
notes.choices:
A) CRI
B) CNI
C) CSI
notes.choicesExplained: A: CRI connects the kubelet to container runtimes. B: CNI is for network plugins.
notes.explanation: CSI allows out-of-tree storage plugins; admins then use the driver through a StorageClass.

notes.front: containerd and CRI-O can each run your Pods’ containers. Which interface makes them interchangeable for the kubelet?
notes.back: CRI, the Container Runtime Interface.
notes.explanation: The kubelet speaks CRI, so any CRI-compatible runtime can serve it.

notes.front: Community members suggest moving a feature out of a plugin and into the core Kubernetes codebase. Are they moving it upstream or downstream?
notes.back: Upstream.
notes.explanation: Upstream is the core codebase the ecosystem relies on; downstream is what builds on it.

notes.front: Someone checks a pull request for backwards compatibility and API conventions, then signs off on merging it. Which role is this?
notes.back: An approver.
notes.explanation: Reviewers focus on code quality and correctness; approvers on holistic acceptance.

notes.front: SIG versus WG: what is the difference?
notes.back: A SIG manages an ongoing area of the project; a WG is a rallying point for a short-lived, narrow or cross-SIG topic.
notes.explanation: SIGs are open to anyone; committees are not.
notes.source: Kubernetes community, “Kubernetes Community Governance Model”, “Working Groups”

notes.front: SIG versus committee: who can join?
notes.back: Anyone can join a SIG, which works in the open; committee membership is closed and decided by the Steering Committee.
notes.explanation: Committees handle topics needing discretion, such as security or code of conduct.

notes.front: Sandbox versus Graduated CNCF project: what separates them?
notes.back: Sandbox is experimental, with breaking changes possible; Graduated is highly mature and proven production-ready by its adopters.
notes.explanation: Incubation sits between them.
notes.source: CNCF TOC, “CNCF Project Lifecycle & Process”, “Project stages”
notes.sourceLicence: C · no licence found; facts in our own words
notes.validAsOf: 2026-09-25 · CNCF documents as of that date

notes.front: Reviewer versus approver: what does each judge?
notes.back: A reviewer checks code quality and correctness; an approver judges holistic acceptance, such as compatibility and conventions.
notes.explanation: Both roles are scoped to part of the codebase.

notes.front: Upstream versus downstream: what is the difference?
notes.back: Upstream is core Kubernetes, or the source repository; downstream is what depends on it, or the fork.
notes.explanation: Features move upstream into the core; the ecosystem adopts them downstream.
